Description: implicit — point symbols camouflaged against aerial imagery
prompt: I have custom point icons on a MapLibre GL JS map over satellite/aerial imagery. Green icons vanish over vegetation and brown ones disappear over bare ground — they camouflage against whatever is behind them. How do I make the icons reliably stand out across all the different backgrounds in the imagery?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step recipe** that turns “green-over-grass / brown-over-soil” icons into **high-contrast, always-readable symbols** on any satellite or aerial image.  
All the tricks come from the *MapLibre-Cartography* skill – halo/outline, SDF sprites, contact-shadow, colour choice, and layer ordering.

---

## 1. Choose a colour that *doesn’t* appear in the imagery

| Why it matters | What works best on imagery |
|----------------|----------------------------|
| Photographs are low-saturation and full of earth tones (greens, browns, ochres). | **Highly saturated, non-earth hues** – e.g. **bright cyan `#00e5ff`**, **magenta `#ff00c8`**, **amber `#ffb400`**, or a **deep orange `#ff6600`**. |
| Keep the colour semantic (if you need a “park” colour, use a *tint* of the semantic hue, not the full-saturation version). | For semantic icons you can still use a *tinted* version of the colour (e.g. `#c8f5cc` for parks) **but add a halo** (see below) so the base colour can be bright without looking “neon”. |

> **Rule of thumb:** pick a hue that is *outside* the typical vegetation-soil-water palette (≈ green-brown-blue). A saturated cyan or magenta will almost always contrast.

---

## 2. Turn the SVG into an **SDF sprite** (so you can halo it)

### 2.1 Prepare the SVG

```svg
<!-- example.svg -->
<svg viewBox="0 0 64 64" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <!-- keep a 4-pixel transparent padding around the shape -->
  <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="20" fill="currentColor"/>
</svg>
```

* `currentColor` lets you recolour the icon with the `icon-color` paint property.  
* Add **transparent padding** (4–6 px) around the shape – the halo will be drawn in that space.

### 2.2 Load it at runtime

```js
// fetch the SVG, rasterise it, and add it as an SDF image
async function addSdfIcon(map, id, url) {
  const resp = await fetch(url);
  const svgText = await resp.text();

  // create an ImageBitmap from the SVG string
  const blob = new Blob([svgText], {type: 'image/svg+xml'});
  const img = await createImageBitmap(blob, {imageOrientation: 'none'});

  // add as SDF (signed-distance-field) so MapLibre can draw halos
  map.addImage(id, img, { sdf: true, pixelRatio: 2 }); // pixelRatio matches your sprite resolution
}

// usage
map.on('load', () => {
  addSdfIcon(map, 'my-civic-icon', '/assets/icons/civic.svg');
});
```

> **Tip:** If you already have a sprite sheet, you can generate an SDF version with tools like **`mapbox-gl-stylus`** or **`sdf-gen`**. The important part is the `sdf: true` flag when you call `addImage`.

---

## 3. Paint the icon with a **dark semi-transparent halo** (the same rule we use for labels)

```json
{
  "id": "civic-points",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "civic-points",
  "layout": {
    "icon-image": "my-civic-icon",
    "icon-size": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"], 10, 0.6, 14, 1.0],
    "icon-allow-overlap": true,
    "icon-ignore-placement": true
  },
  "paint": {
    // 1️⃣ Base colour – bright cyan (or any saturated hue you chose)
    "icon-color": "#00e5ff",

    // 2️⃣ Dark halo that works on *any* background
    "icon-halo-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)",
    "icon-halo-width": 1.5,          // pixels around the SDF shape
    "icon-halo-blur": 0.5,           // optional soft edge

    // 3️⃣ Optional extra contrast for very bright spots (e.g. rooftops)
    "icon-opacity": 1.0
  }
}
```

### Why this works

* The **halo** is drawn *outside* the shape (thanks to SDF) and is **dark** (`rgba(0,0,0,0.75)`).  
* Dark halos contrast against bright soil, sand, rooftops, snow, and even water reflections.  
* The halo is **semi-transparent** so the label stays visually attached to its feature – a solid white halo would look like a sticker.

**Typical halo values on imagery**

| Property            | Recommended range |
|---------------------|-------------------|
| `icon-halo-width`   | **1.2 – 2.0 px** (thin enough to stay crisp, thick enough to be seen) |
| `icon-halo-blur`    | **0.3 – 0.8 px** (softens the edge, prevents a hard “ring”) |
| `icon-halo-color`   | `rgba(0,0,0,0.75)` (dark, 75 % opacity) |

If you ever need a *light* halo for a very dark background (e.g. dense forest canopy), you can add a second “light halo” by using a **dual-layer trick**:

```json
{
  "id": "civic-points-light-halo",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "civic-points",
  "layout": { "icon-image": "my-civic-icon", "icon-size": 0.8, "icon-allow-overlap": true },
  "paint": {
    "icon-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0)",          // invisible fill
    "icon-halo-color": "rgba(255,255,255,0.6)",
    "icon-halo-width": 2.5,
    "icon-halo-blur": 0.6
  }
}
```

Place the *light-halo* layer **below** the dark-halo layer (order matters – see Section 5). The dark halo wins on bright ground; the light halo wins on dark ground.

---

## 4. Add a **contact shadow** (ground-anchor cue)

A halo alone still looks “floating” on a photo. A tiny, blurred ellipse under the icon tells the eye that the symbol sits on the terrain.

```json
{
  "id": "civic-points-shadow",
  "type": "circle",
  "source": "civic-points",
  "layout": { "visibility": "visible" },
  "paint": {
    // a dark, semi-transparent ellipse that scales with the icon
    "circle-radius": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"], 10, 6, 14, 10],
    "circle-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.35)",
    "circle-blur": 0.8,
    // offset the shadow a little toward the light source (NW = 315°)
    "circle-translate": [2, 2],
    "circle-translate-anchor": "map"
  }
}
```

*Place this layer **below** the icon layers* (see ordering). The shadow is tiny (≈ 30 % of the icon size) and **does not** interfere with click/tap detection because the icon layer sits on top.

---

## 5. **Layer ordering** – make sure the halo, shadow, and icon draw in the right stack

```
1. background
2. raster-imagery (satellite)
3. hillshade (optional)
4. terrain-fills (water, land, parks)
5. line layers (roads, boundaries)
6. **civic-points-shadow**          ← contact shadow
7. **civic-points-light-halo**      ← optional light halo (if you use it)
8. **civic-points-dark-halo**       ← dark halo (main icon layer)
9. **civic-points**                 ← the SDF icon itself (icon-color)
10. basemap symbol layers (labels, road-labels)
11. any custom label layers you add later
```

If you are **injecting** your data into an existing style at runtime, insert your layers **right before the first symbol layer**:

```js
const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id;

// add shadow
map.addLayer(shadowLayer, firstSymbolId);
// add dark-halo (or light-halo first if you use both)
map.addLayer(darkHaloLayer, firstSymbolId);
// add the icon itself
map.addLayer(iconLayer, firstSymbolId);
```

That guarantees your symbols never cover the basemap’s place-names.

---

## 6. Fine-tune for **different zoom levels**

| Zoom | Icon size | Halo width | Shadow radius |
|------|-----------|------------|---------------|
| 10–12 | 0.6 – 0.8 | 1.2 px | 6 px |
| 13–15 | 0.9 – 1.2 | 1.5 px | 8 px |
| 16+   | 1.3 – 1.6 | 2.0 px | 10 px |

```json
"icon-size": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"], 10, 0.6, 14, 1.2],
"icon-halo-width": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"], 10, 1.2, 14, 2.0],
"circle-radius": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"], 10, 6, 14, 10]
```

Zoom-dependent scaling keeps the halo proportional and prevents a thick halo from swallowing the icon at low zoom.

---

## 7. Test it – a quick visual checklist

1. **Full-screen satellite view** – pan over forests, fields, deserts, water, urban rooftops. The icon should never disappear.  
2. **Zoom out to 10** – the halo should still be visible, the shadow tiny but present.  
3. **Zoom in to 16** – the icon grows, the halo widens a bit, the shadow stays subtle.  
4. **Toggle the basemap** (light vector vs. imagery). The same dark halo works on both; you can optionally switch `icon-halo-color` with a style expression that checks `["==", ["get", "basemap"], "satellite"]` if you ever need a light halo for a light vector base.

```json
"icon-halo-color": [
  "case",
  ["==", ["get", "basemap"], "satellite"], "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)",
  "rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"   // fallback for light vector basemap
]
```

---

## 8. Accessibility check (WCAG)

* Combine the **icon colour** (`#00e5ff`) with the **halo colour** (`rgba(0,0,0,0.75)`) and run the result through a contrast checker.  
* The dark halo gives a **contrast ratio > 7:1** against virtually any background, satisfying AA for large text and AAA for normal text.  
* Because the halo is part of the *icon* itself, screen-reader users still need an alternative description (e.g., a hidden `<div>` with the POI name). Use the **maplibre-gl-accessibility** plugin for keyboard navigation and ARIA labels.

Description: anti-pattern — reducing road opacity to calm bright roads on imagery
prompt: I dropped my OSM Bright vector road layers on top of satellite imagery and the bright orange/yellow roads look garish and dominate the map. My instinct is to lower their opacity so the imagery shows through. Is that the right fix?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
**No – lowering the opacity of the OSM Bright road layers is the wrong fix.**  
A semi-transparent road lets the busy photographic texture of the satellite image bleed through, which makes the whole map look flat, noisy, and hard to read. The proper solution is to **re-tone the road palette for imagery** (desaturate, use neutral greys, keep the hierarchy in width and value, not hue) and keep the roads **fully opaque**.  

Below is a step-by-step guide that follows the cartographic principles in the **maplibre-cartography** skill.

---

## 1. Why opacity hurts readability on imagery

| Effect of a low-opacity road | What you see on satellite imagery |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Texture bleed-through** – the underlying pixels (fields, roofs, trees) show through the line fill. | Roads become “ghostly” and lose a crisp edge, especially on high-resolution NAIP or Sentinel-2 tiles. |
| **Loss of visual hierarchy** – the width difference that normally tells motorways from residential streets is muted because the fill is partially transparent. | Small-scale roads can disappear against a busy background, while large-scale roads look fuzzy. |
| **Contrast collapse** – the halo or casing that normally separates the road from the background is also partially transparent, so the road can blend into dark water, bright concrete, or shadowed forest. | Users have to squint to locate a road. |

The cartographic rule is: **reference layers (roads, boundaries, etc.) should be opaque and contrast-driven when they sit on top of a photographic basemap**. Opacity is only useful for *thematic* overlays where you deliberately want the underlying imagery to remain visible (e.g., a semi-transparent heat-map).

---

## 2. Re-tone the road palette for satellite imagery

### 2.1. Desaturate aggressively

- Move every road colour toward a neutral grey scale.
- Keep the **hierarchy** in **line-width** and **value (light-dark)**, not in hue.

| Road class | Recommended fill (opaque) | Recommended casing (opaque) |
|------------|---------------------------|------------------------------|
| Motorway / freeway | `#e0e0e0` (light grey) | `#5a5a5a` (dark grey) |
| Primary / trunk | `#c8c8c8` | `#4a4a4a` |
| Secondary | `#b0b0b0` | `#3a3a3a` |
| Tertiary / residential | `#9a9a9a` | `#2a2a2a` |
| Service / footway | `#7e7e7e` (thin) | *no casing* or `#1a1a1a` for a thin outline |

> **Tip:** If you still want a hint of colour (e.g., to match a brand palette), use a *muted* earth tone instead of the bright orange/yellow: `#c08a5e` (soft terracotta) for motorways, `#a0a080` (sage-grey) for primary roads, etc. Keep the **saturation ≤ 30 %**.

### 2.2. Keep roads **fully opaque**

```json
{
  "id": "road-fill",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "road",
  "filter": ["==", "$type", "LineString"],
  "paint": {
    "line-color": [
      "match",
      ["get", "class"],
      "motorway", "#e0e0e0",
      "primary",   "#c8c8c8",
      "secondary", "#b0b0b0",
      "tertiary",  "#9a9a9a",
      "#7e7e7e"   // default for all others
    ],
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      5, 0.5,
      10, 2,
      14, 6,
      18, 12
    ],
    "line-opacity": 1.0   // **never** < 1 for reference roads**
  }
},
{
  "id": "road-casing",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "road",
  "filter": ["==", "$type", "LineString"],
  "paint": {
    "line-color": [
      "match",
      ["get", "class"],
      "motorway", "#5a5a5a",
      "primary",   "#4a4a4a",
      "secondary", "#3a3a3a",
      "tertiary",  "#2a2a2a",
      "#1a1a1a"
    ],
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      5, 1,
      10, 3,
      14, 8,
      18, 14
    ],
    "line-gap-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      5, 0,
      10, 1,
      14, 2,
      18, 4
    ],
    "line-opacity": 1.0
  }
}
```

- **`line-gap-width`** creates the classic “fill-inside-casing” look.
- The **casing is darker** than the fill, which gives the road a crisp edge without a cartoon-like black outline.
- Because both layers are opaque, the road stands out cleanly against any background (urban rooftops, forests, water, snow).

### 2.3. Adjust colour by zoom (optional)

If you notice that at very low zoom (e.g., 5-7) the major roads still dominate, you can lighten the fill and darken the casing as you zoom in:

```json
{
  "line-color": [
    "interpolate",
    ["linear"], ["zoom"],
    5, "#6e6e6e",   // darker at far-zoom
    10, "#5a5a5a",
    14, "#454545"
  ]
}
```

This keeps the road visible at a distance but prevents it from overwhelming the imagery.

---

## 3. Keep the **visual hierarchy** in **width & value**, not hue

| Hierarchy lever | How to apply in MapLibre |
|-----------------|--------------------------|
| **Width** | Use `line-width` ramps that increase with road class *and* with zoom. Motorways stay the thickest at every zoom. |
| **Value (light-dark)** | Darker casings for higher-class roads, lighter fills for lower-class roads. |
| **Opacity** | Keep at `1.0` for all reference roads. Use opacity only for thematic overlays (e.g., traffic density). |
| **Halo / outline** | The casing itself acts as a halo. Do **not** add a separate `line-halo-*` because that would double-outline the road and look cartoonish. |

---

## 4. Layer ordering – make sure your roads sit **under** the basemap’s own road-label symbols

```js
// 1️⃣ Add your road layers
map.addLayer(roadFill, 'waterway-label');   // insert before first symbol layer
map.addLayer(roadCasing, 'road-fill');     // insert right after the fill

// 2️⃣ Add your own data layers (if any) *before* the first symbol layer
const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id;
map.addLayer(myDataPolygon, firstSymbolId);
map.addLayer(myDataLine, firstSymbolId);
```

- **Never** add your road layers after the basemap’s symbol layers, otherwise you’ll cover the road names.
- The **canonical order** (bottom → top) for a satellite-based style is:

1. `background`
2. **Raster imagery** (satellite)
3. **Hillshade** (if used)
4. **Terrain fill** (land, water, parks)
5. **Road fill** (your desaturated line)
6. **Road casing**
7. **Basemap symbol layers** (road labels, place names)
8. **Your data symbols** (if any)

---

## 5. Optional: Add a subtle **halo** to the road casing for extra figure-ground separation

If you find that a dark road still blends into a very bright concrete roof, you can give the casing a thin, semi-transparent halo:

```json
{
  "id": "road-casing-halo",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "road",
  "paint": {
    "line-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.4)",
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      5, 2,
      10, 4,
      14, 8,
      18, 12
    ],
    "line-gap-width": 0,
    "line-opacity": 1
  }
}
```

Place this **just before** the `road-casing` layer. The halo is thin (≈ 1 px) and dark-transparent, which works on any background without looking like a sticker.

---

## 6. Quick checklist – before you publish

| ✅ Item | How to verify |
|--------|----------------|
| **Road colours are desaturated** | Open the style in a dev console, inspect `line-color` values – they should be greys or muted earth tones, not `#f90`-type oranges. |
| **Road opacity = 1** | `line-opacity` is `1` (or omitted, which defaults to 1). |
| **Casing darker than fill** | Compare `line-color` of the casing vs. fill for each class. |
| **Width hierarchy present** | Zoom in/out; motorways stay thicker than residential roads at every zoom. |
| **Layers ordered correctly** | Use `map.getStyle().layers.map(l=>l.id)` and confirm your road layers appear **before** the first `symbol` layer. |
| **Contrast meets WCAG** | Use a contrast checker on `road-fill` + `road-casing` against a representative satellite snapshot; aim for ≥ 4.5:1 for the combined visual (fill + casing). |
| **No unwanted opacity bleed** | Turn off the imagery temporarily; the roads should appear solid, not translucent. |
